content: Preterm birth is the primary cause of mortality in newborns and children. Tocolytic drugs are used to delay preterm labor by suppressing uterine contractions. This delay allows time for the administration of corticosteroids to promote fetal lung maturation, magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection, and the transfer of the mother to a facility equipped with appropriate neonatal care. However, the effectiveness and safety of these drugs remain uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the relative effectiveness and safety of different classes of tocolytic drugs in delaying preterm birth and to rank the available options. A comprehensive search was conducted in databases such as Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth’s Trials Register and ClinicalTrials.gov, up to April 21, 2021. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included, while quasi-randomized and non-randomized trials were excluded. The included studies were assessed for trustworthiness based on predefined criteria. A total of 122 trials involving 13,697 women were included in this network meta-analysis. These trials evaluated six classes of tocolytic drugs, combinations of tocolytics, and placebo or no treatment. Most studies involved women with threatened preterm labor between 24 and 34 weeks of gestation. Twenty-five studies (20%) were judged to have a low risk of bias. The certainty of the evidence varied across the studies. The analysis suggested that all tocolytics are likely effective in delaying preterm birth compared to placebo or no treatment. Betamimetics may delay preterm birth by 48 hours (risk ratio [RR] 1.12, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.05 to 1.20; low-certainty evidence) and by 7 days (RR 1.14, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.25; low-certainty evidence). Cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibitors may also delay preterm birth by 48 hours (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.23; low-certainty evidence). Calcium channel blockers may delay preterm birth by 48 hours (RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.24; low-certainty evidence) and are probably effective in delaying preterm birth by 7 days (RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.27; moderate-certainty evidence). They may also prolong pregnancy by an average of 5 days (high-certainty evidence). Magnesium sulfate is probably effective in delaying preterm birth by 48 hours (RR 1.12, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.23; moderate-certainty evidence). Oxytocin receptor antagonists are likely effective in delaying preterm birth by 48 hours (RR 1.13, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.22; moderate-certainty evidence) and by 7 days (RR 1.18, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.30; high-certainty evidence). They may also prolong pregnancy by 10 days (95% CI 2.3 to 16.7 days). Nitric oxide donors are probably effective in delaying preterm birth by 48 hours (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.31; moderate-certainty evidence) and by 7 days (RR 1.18, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.37; moderate-certainty evidence). Combinations of tocolytics are likely effective in delaying preterm birth by 48 hours (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.27; moderate-certainty evidence) and by 7 days (RR 1.19, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.34; moderate-certainty evidence). Among the tocolytics, nitric oxide donors ranked highest for delaying preterm birth by 48 hours and 7 days, followed by calcium channel blockers, oxytocin receptor antagonists, and combinations of tocolytics. Betamimetics, calcium channel blockers, magnesium sulfate, and combinations of tocolytics were more likely to result in cessation of treatment due to adverse effects. Calcium channel blockers may reduce the risk of neurodevelopmental morbidity (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.85; low-certainty evidence) and respiratory morbidity (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.88; low-certainty evidence). They may also result in fewer neonates with a birth weight below 2000 g (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.87; low-certainty evidence). Nitric oxide donors may result in neonates with higher birth weights (mean difference [MD] 425.53 g, 95% CI 224.32 to 626.74 g; low-certainty evidence), fewer neonates with a birth weight below 2500 g (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.69; low-certainty evidence), and more advanced gestational age (MD 1.35 weeks, 95% CI 0.37 to 2.32 weeks; low-certainty evidence). Combinations of tocolytics may result in fewer neonates with a birth weight below 2500 g (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.93; low-certainty evidence). Regarding maternal adverse effects, betamimetics are likely to cause dyspnea (RR 12.09, 95% CI 4.66 to 31.39; moderate-certainty evidence), palpitations (RR 7.39, 95% CI 3.83 to 14.24; moderate-certainty evidence), vomiting (RR 1.91, 95% CI 1.25 to 2.91; moderate-certainty evidence), and possibly headache (RR 1.91, 95% CI 1.07 to 3.42; low-certainty evidence) and tachycardia (RR 3.01, 95% CI 1.17 to 7.71; low-certainty evidence). COX inhibitors may cause vomiting (RR 2.54, 95% CI 1.18 to 5.48; low-certainty evidence). Calcium channel blockers and nitric oxide donors are likely to cause headaches (RR 2.59, 95% CI 1.39 to 4.83; low-certainty evidence and RR 4.20, 95% CI 2.13 to 8.25; moderate-certainty evidence, respectively). In conclusion, all assessed tocolytic drug classes (betamimetics, calcium channel blockers, magnesium sulfate, oxytocin receptor antagonists, nitric oxide donors) and their combinations are likely or possibly effective in delaying preterm birth by 48 hours and 7 days compared to placebo or no treatment. However, the use of tocolytics is associated with a range of adverse effects, from minor to potentially severe. Betamimetics and combination tocolytics are more likely to lead to treatment cessation. The impact of tocolytics on neonatal outcomes, such as neonatal and perinatal mortality, and safety outcomes, such as maternal and neonatal infections, remains uncertain.
